text: Cassini was the biggest spacecraft ever sent to another planet: 6.7 m tall, about two stories, and 5.6 metric tons at launch.
Cassini was too heavy to fly straight to Saturn. It spent nearly seven years getting there, slingshotting past Venus twice, then Earth, then Jupiter, to pick up speed.
Cassini was the first spacecraft ever to orbit Saturn. To get captured, it fired its main engine for 96 minutes on arrival in July 2004.
Cassini had no solar panels. Three nuclear generators turned the heat of decaying plutonium-238 into electricity.
Cassini spent 13 years orbiting Saturn, nearly half a Saturn year, long enough to watch the seasons change.
In January 2005 the Huygens probe parachuted onto Titan. It is still the only landing ever made on a world in the outer solar system.
After landing on Titan, Huygens ran on batteries and kept sending data for another 72 minutes.
The small moon Enceladus is spraying water vapor and ice into space from warm cracks at its south pole. Cassini caught it in the act in 2005.
Titan has lakes and seas on its surface, but they are liquid methane and other hydrocarbons, not water. Cassini mapped them by radar through the haze.
Saturn's north pole is ringed by a hexagon: a six-sided jet stream wider than the whole Earth.
On 19 July 2013 Cassini hid in Saturn's shadow and photographed Earth as a tiny dot beyond the rings, while people back home were invited to wave at Saturn.
Every picture in the camera windows comes from one of Cassini's two cameras: the narrow-angle telephoto (NAC) and the wide-angle (WAC).
Giovanni Cassini found the big dark gap in Saturn's rings that still bears his name. Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655. The spacecraft and its probe are named after them.
Cassini found new moons hiding in and near the rings, among them Methone, Pallene, Daphnis, Anthe and Aegaeon.
In its last five months Cassini dived 22 times through the gap between Saturn and its rings, where no spacecraft had ever been.
Cassini's ending was on purpose: it was steered into Saturn so it could never crash into Enceladus or Titan and contaminate them.
Cassini kept sending science during its final plunge, for as long as its thrusters could keep the antenna pointed at Earth. The last signal reached Australia on 15 September 2017.
